findings.printedLatin: Quomodo inquinabo illos? id est, quomodo fieri potest, ut iterum ad cogitanda caduca et terrena redeam, quae nunc in occupato et libero corde divino fruor contuitu?
findings.englishAsRendered: how can it come about that I should return again to thinking upon perishable and earthly things, I who now, in an occupied and free heart, enjoy the divine gaze?
findings.conjecture: in <in>occupato et libero corde (or non occupato) — 'in an unoccupied and free heart'
findings.whyContradiction: 'occupato' contradicts its own coordinate adjective 'libero' in the same phrase, and contradicts the soul's own account two sentences earlier: 'Exui me curis et occupationibus hujus saeculi' and 'adeo ut nihil nunc nisi divina me libeat cogitare.' The whole point of the gloss is that she is NOT occupied — that is why she fears re-entanglement ('iterum occupationibus saeculi implicetur').

findings.printedLatin: Lavi pedes meos, hoc est, actiones quibus nunquam pulverem [1082D] tangere, hoc est, terrena agere consueveram, dignis poenitentiae fletibus ablui
findings.englishAsRendered: I have washed my feet, that is, the actions with which I was never accustomed to touch the dust, that is, to do earthly things, I have washed with the worthy weeping of penance
findings.conjecture: quibus quondam (or unquam / aliquando) pulverem tangere ... consueveram
findings.whyContradiction: The clause exists to explain why the feet needed washing 'dignis poenitentiae fletibus'; actions that NEVER touched dust require no tears of penance. The lemma itself is 'Lavi pedes meos, quomodo inquinabo illos?' — feet that were dirty and are now clean.

findings.printedLatin: Timet ergo Ecclesia vel anima quaeque sancta hac tunica exui, et in contemplatione sui Conditoris requiescens, iterum reindui et saecularibus negotiis occupari.
findings.englishAsRendered: The Church, therefore, or every holy soul, fears to be stripped of this garment, and, resting in the contemplation of her Maker, to be clothed again and taken up with worldly business.
findings.conjecture: hac tunica exuta ... iterum reindui timet — 'the Church, stripped of this tunic and resting in contemplation, fears to be clothed again'
findings.whyContradiction: The tunic has just been defined as 'curis et occupationibus hujus saeculi', and the bride's own words are 'Exspoliavi me tunica mea: quomodo induar illa?' — she boasts of the stripping and dreads the reclothing. As printed she fears the very act she performed, and the sentence then also makes her fear reclothing, i.e. fears both opposites.

findings.printedLatin: sed plerumque fidelem animam se desiderantem, et ad se venire cupientem non exaudit, ad hoc ut ita se ei praesenti ostendat, sicut se in futurum ostensurum promittit
findings.englishAsRendered: but very often he does not hear the faithful soul that desires him and longs to come to him, to this end, that he may so show himself to it as present as he promises he will show himself in the time to come
findings.conjecture: ad hoc ut non ita se ei praesenti ostendat, sicut se in futurum ostensurum promittit
findings.whyContradiction: Its immediate neighbour a few lines earlier denies exactly this equivalence: 'quia nemo eum in praesenti vita, sicuti est, comprehendere potest' (1083C), and at 1090A the same author writes 'Non enim videbit me homo, et vivet ... Cum autem vinculis carnis absoluta ad me perveneris, tunc me aperta visione videbis.' As printed, the reason he does NOT hear is that he may show himself now just as he promises to show himself hereafter.

findings.printedLatin: Exspectabat enim manentem civitatem, cujus conditor et artifex Deus est [n: (Hebr. XI, 10)]
findings.englishAsRendered: For he looked for a city that hath foundations, whose builder and craftsman is God
findings.conjecture: 'For he looked for the abiding city, whose founder and craftsman is God' — Migne prints *manentem*, not the Vulgate's *fundamenta habentem*; the familiar English ('a city that hath foundations') has been imported over the printed word.
findings.whyContradiction: Not a contradiction but a silent substitution of the received English lemma for the printed Latin: the printed text has no word for 'foundations' at all. The English also silently restores the Vulgate word-order 'artifex et conditor' → 'builder and craftsman' while Migne prints 'conditor et artifex'.

findings.printedLatin: Contra Damascum ergo est haec turris: quia haec Ecclesia semper diabolo et membris illius, adjutorio Christi munita, resistit.
findings.englishAsRendered: This tower therefore is toward Damascus: because this Church, fortified by the help of Christ, always resists the devil and his members.
findings.conjecture: 'This tower therefore is AGAINST Damascus: because ... always resists the devil and his members.'
findings.whyContradiction: The causal clause the English itself prints ('because ... always resists') only follows from an adversative 'contra'. Damascus has just been glossed as 'potestates hujus saeculi, quae sanguinis potum sitiunt' and 'aeras potestates, quae animarum nostrarum cruorem sitiunt' — the tower does not face them neutrally, it stands against them. The neutral 'toward' (right for the lemma's *respicit contra Damascum*) is carried over into the concluding sentence, where it drains the adversative force the gloss depends on.
